the acoustic emission (AE) signal generated by low-velocity (less-than 0.21km/s) impacts in thin aluminum and composite plates is dominated by a large amplitude flexural mode with a small extensional component.
the AE signals from low-velocity impacts in thin plates are characterized by large-amplitude, long-duration, flexural waves.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an acoustic emission technique for the detection and location of impact damage in composite materials.
the acoustic emission signals generated by impact damage in thin plates and the relationship between these signals and the type of damage produced.
the development of a new nondestructive technique for the evaluation of impact damage in thin composite structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amplitude and frequency of the acoustic emission signal are functions of both the velocity and angle of the impact.
AE signals caused by high-impact velocities are more complex than those generated by low-impact velocities.
the acoustic emission signals produced by impact damage in thin aluminum and composite plates are very different from those generated by other types of damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
low-velocity impacts generate signals that are dominated by a large-amplitude flexural mode component.
AE can be used to distinguish low- and high-velocity impacts, and can detect both the presence and absence of penetration in composite plates.
the AE signals caused by high- velocity impacts are much larger in amplitude and have a much wider frequency range than those caused by low velocity impacts.

the AE signal characteristics depend strongly on both the impact velocity and the impact angle.
the AE signal is a very sensitive indicator of the impact velocity and the damage caused by the impact.
